items.item: An engine-side policy is strictly stronger than an application-side one because it is checked at the point a row or column is read, regardless of which application sent the query — an application-side check only ever covers requests that pass through that one application's own code.

items.item: A pushed-down row policy changes the number of rows the engine ever examines, not just the number returned; the cost difference is visible in a plan's own rows-examined counter, which Chapter 2's triage order already teaches how to read.

items.item: A materialized view, an export, and a direct file read all fail for the same underlying reason: none of them re-run the policy's evaluation, because none of them send a new query against the live, policy-attached table.

items.item: Topic 5's file-level encryption is the only one of this topic's own controls that actually reaches a direct file read, because it protects the bytes themselves rather than relying on a query ever being asked.

items.item: The policy this topic enforces mechanically is the same one topic 7 designed in the abstract — the decision/enforcement split topic 7 introduces is what lets one engine-side check serve row filtering, column masking, and more, all through the same evaluated rule.

A mask or filter is always written against a tag or tier already applied at classification time; without that earlier classification step, there is no attribute for a row or column policy to read in the first place.
Reading a plan's rows-examined counter before and after adding a policy is the same triage skill Chapter 2 teaches generally, applied here to one specific question: did the filter get pushed down.

The five engines named in the syllabus clause differ in vocabulary (masking policy, row filter, data filter, OPA endpoint) but not in the underlying guarantee each one's own documentation states: the rule is evaluated by the engine, against the live table, at the moment of the read.
